candidates.title: Can AI Models Learn to Recognize When They Don’t Know the Answer?
candidates.summary:
Hi everyone!

We often focus on making AI models more accurate, faster, and more capable, but I’m curious about a different challenge: teaching models to recognize when they might be wrong.

For example, could a model estimate its own uncertainty well enough to say, “I’m not confident about this answer,” instead of generating something that sounds convincing but is incorrect?

candidates.title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
candidates.summary: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. candidates.title: Tev: Scaling Long-Horizon Agentic Environments with Dense Progress Rewards
candidates.summary: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards

candidates.title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
candidates.summary: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density.

candidates.summary: Learning humanoid loco-manipulation from human demonstrations rests on observing how locomotion, posture, and object interaction evolve together as tasks unfold. Scaling collection across diverse environments, in turn, favors lightweight, portable capture systems. Yet, existing datasets provide only partial views of this coordination.
